hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named FSL Pitcher of the Week
hero.teaser: The 22-year-old left-hander struck out 12 batters over seven scoreless innings in two appearances against Fort Myers.
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced Monday.

Ware made two appearances against the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels at Clover Park, starting Tuesday and returning for a relief outing Sunday. The left-hander combined to throw seven scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two walks while striking out 12 batters.

The Mets won both games in which Ware appeared. He earned the victory Sunday after pitching four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk and recording a career-high eight strikeouts as St. Lucie rallied for an 11-8 win.

Ware, 22, was selected by the New York Mets in the 15th round of the 2025 MLB Draft out of LSU. He made his professional debut with St. Lucie in April and has remained with the team throughout the season.

cards.headline: Leon County judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor. Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election. During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence.

Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory or more severe legal repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida. He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump.

Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent. The judge also pointed to Fishback's Florida upbringing, family relationships, driver's license, vehicle registration, voting history and work with Incubate Debate, a statewide nonprofit operating student debate programs throughout Florida. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings. Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station on Tradition commercial site after months of resident concerns
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a permanent ban on gas stations at a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive on July 13. The restriction came after months of debate over a request by Winding River Crosstown LLC to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. While council members supported adding commercial uses to the rapidly growing area, several voiced concerns during the initial May 26 hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95.

The council tabled the request in May after Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel. When the hearing resumed June 22, several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. The council voted 4-0 to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station.

The updated development plan now specifies that while service stations remain permitted elsewhere within the Tradition mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. The city also added protections requested by nearby residents. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. An architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction.

City planner Bridget Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. Councilman Anthony Bonna said he believes expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city's tax base. Councilman David Pickett said going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner. The amendment changes the parcel's designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development.

cards.headline: TPS expiration leaves Haitian workers in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce without jobs
cards.teaser: Temporary Protected Status expired Monday for Haitian immigrants, stripping workers of jobs and disrupting schools and public services across the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Valentina Lorissaint said many relatives and friends are already unable to work after losing authorization tied to TPS. She said a lot of people have been scared, just wondering what the next meal they're going to eat the next day. Residents described widespread anxiety rippling through the community, with some families afraid to leave their homes or send children to school.

Chuck Ridley, director of civic engagement for the Service Employees International Union, said the union expects hundreds of workers statewide to be affected, including nearly 20 employees in the Palm Beach County School District alone. The Palm Beach County School District said 19 District employees will be separated from employment as all School District employees must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Ridley said many of the workers losing TPS protections are bus drivers, custodians, paraprofessionals, food service employees and city workers.

The Florida Healthcare Association said Haitian caregivers are valued members of the long term care workforce, serving as certified nursing assistants, nurses, dietary aides, housekeepers and other essential team members. According to the Lar Management Group, the Haitian community contributes an estimated $1.2 billion to Florida's economy. TPS allows people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other unsafe conditions to live and work temporarily in the United States. The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory for Haiti, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County families say Florida Medicaid abruptly cut autism therapy for children
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it. Florida's health agency has not explained why.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to a critical autism therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it and Florida's health agency has not explained why. The therapy at the center of the dispute is Applied Behavioral Analysis, or ABA. The Cleveland Clinic describes it as a research-based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders, adding that many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA. Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment.

Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said her son David is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described the progress he had made through ABA, saying his vocabulary have been increasingly amazing and he can understand what is happening. Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions. Since the therapy stopped, Talia Quiroz said she has experienced dangerous regressions in her daughter's behavior. Suarez described similar physical consequences, saying she has bruised arms from one of her son's pinching.

Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country. The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Colorado. Its findings identified roughly $200 million in what it considers improper payments among the four states. A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over, across a five-year period. Questions were sent to Florida's Agency for Healthcare Administration, which runs the state's Medicaid program.

cards.headline: Indiantown Council rejects pause on data center applications despite resident pressure
cards.body:
A pair of Indiantown Village Council members failed to gain support Monday for a 90-day pause on data center applications, with village officials citing concerns about violating state law and risking millions in state funding. Councilwoman Karen Onsager proposed an administrative pause on accepting, processing and approving new applications for large-load data center development projects. The motion came after civic activist Melissa Hague renewed her request from June, telling the Council that not pausing to review land development regulations would be negligent.

Village Attorney Wade Vose said the pause would violate Senate Bills 180 and 484, repeating his legal opinion from June that such a move would put Indiantown at risk of lawsuits from property owners and developers. Vose told the Council he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney representing multiple developers within the village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit any regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed that industrially zoned lands within the village allow data centers as a permitted use.

Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer supported the concept but wanted a longer timeframe of 12 to 18 months rather than 90 days. Onsager said she chose 90 days specifically to avoid running afoul of state law and because the village is in the middle of an election cycle. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned against offending state officials who have given Indiantown over $120 million in funding. Kryzda added that when local government goes against the state or federal government, the first thing they look to do is withhold funding.

No council member seconded Onsager's motion, causing it to die. The proposal followed the withdrawal in April of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which had drawn protests from scores of local residents. Kryzda confirmed that the community meeting Onsager requested will be scheduled for Saturday, August 2, and will include technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, utility providers and relevant staff.

cards.headline: Armed robbers force victim to withdraw cash at Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Two men forced a victim to withdraw cash at gunpoint from a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce Sunday night before fleeing on foot.
cards.body:
A man using a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce became the victim of an armed robbery Sunday night when two men forced him to withdraw cash before fleeing on foot. The Fort Pierce Police Department reported the incident occurred at approximately 8:38 p.m.

Two men approached the victim while he was at the ATM. One of the suspects displayed a gun that was concealed in his waistband and forced the victim to withdraw cash. The amount of money taken remains unknown. After obtaining the cash, both suspects fled the scene on foot.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the robbery and established a perimeter around the area. Law enforcement deployed both a K-9 unit and a drone to search for the suspects. Despite these efforts, the suspects were not located.

Police described both suspects as men in their early 20s, standing approximately 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing around 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt. The Fort Pierce Police Department is investigating the incident.

hero.headline: Cyclist rides through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Maine
hero.teaser: A Boston cyclist rode through Vero Beach this week on a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine to honor a friend lost to colorectal cancer.
hero.body:
Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin the journey, with a goal of raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach, after filling his hydration pack with ice to stay cool.

Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day up the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County commissioners deadlock on infrastructure tax renewal, postpone decision
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision u
cards.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision until August 4. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation.

 Before the commission's discussion on July 21, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Port St. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek said there is a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life. Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year.

 Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot, saying he did not want it on the same ballot as Amendment 3 and the School Board tax. Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word tax. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote.

 With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until August 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist begins 2,600-mile ride from Key West to Maine to honor friend lost to colorectal cancer
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine with a goal of raising $50,000 for young-onset colorectal cancer research.
cards.body:
A Boston cyclist is turning heartbreak into hope. After losing a close friend to young-onset colorectal cancer, Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine, with a goal of raising $50,000 for research while honoring his friend's memory. The death of his friend, who was also named Jay, inspired Weedall to honor his memory by riding his bike across the country. His goal is to raise $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center in honor of the friend he lost to the disease.

 To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned for the long journey ahead. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach.

 Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day along the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine.

 By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along those inlets. When riding hundreds of miles alone, Weedall says he has plenty of time to think. He said that even when his legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when he is a little anxious about what is going on around him, he is largely just thinking about his friend who does not get the opportunity to do this with him anymore. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council lowered the city's millage rate to 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, down from 4.9750, continuing an 11-year trend of property tax reductions.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council agreed to lower the city's property tax millage rate for the 11th consecutive year at the annual Summer Workshop held July 22-23. The Council approved a millage rate of 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, a decrease from 4.9750 in fiscal year 2025-26. The budget will be adopted by City Council in September, with public hearings taking place Sept. 4 and Sept. 18, and goes into effect Oct. 1.

 Since 2016, the city has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, saving the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over a 10-year period. Port St. Lucie has the third lowest municipal tax rate out of Florida's 20 largest cities. The property tax reduction maintains Port St. Lucie's record of steadily reducing its millage rate while managing historic population growth, investing in essential infrastructure and improving public safety.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie opens $28.8 million police training center with 20-lane indoor firing range
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie cut the ribbon on a three-story, 54,283-square-foot police training facility on the City Hall grounds featuring advanced virtual reality technology and indoor firearms capabilities.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie officially opened its $28.8 million police training center on July 24 with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on the City Hall grounds just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, three-story facility was four years in construction and was designed by ADG Architecture and built by HJ High. Mayor Shannon Martin said the project ensures officers have the space, training, and resources needed to serve the community at the highest level.

 The facility includes a 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range with an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system, a 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms, and a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for decision-making and de-escalation exercises. It also features a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology, a multi-purpose training room, and three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division with 19 offices and 86 workstations.

 Officer Brittany McNally said the facility will reduce recurring costs from officers traveling to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for training. The new training center provides access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic scenario-based training that better prepares officers for situations they may face in the field, she said. Police personnel immediately began moving into the facility after the ribbon cutting. The facility is not open to the general public due to safety and confidentiality concerns.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County sees highest home price increase on Treasure Coast, up 2.3% to $399,000
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Prices have dropped for condos and townhomes in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

cards.headline: Suspect found hiding on roof after 80 mph chase through Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver and his passenger fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph before abandoning their car and running, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. The driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. The driver and passenger weaved in and out of traffic, ignored traffic signs and signals, then abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home. Joseph Gary Harris, 42, was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Bryan Shawn Baker, 46, was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighter Geoffrey Lang dies off duty
cards.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue is mourning Firefighter and Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died while off duty Saturday night.
cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue announced the death of Firefighter and Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died while off duty Saturday night. The department called it a regretful loss and asked the community to keep his loved ones in their thoughts. Indian River County Fire Rescue thanked neighboring agencies that quickly shared messages of support following the announcement.

The Sebastian Police Department said it was joining Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning Lang's death and wrote that his bravery and service will always be remembered. The Vero Beach Police Department also shared its condolences, saying it stands alongside the fire department during the difficult time. Indian River County Fire Rescue said additional information will be released in the coming days.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce neighbor says she fed hungry children from mobile home where infant died
cards.teaser: A neighbor across the street from the Fort Pierce mobile home where a 3-month-old died said she gave food and water to other children from the home who appeared hungry and unbathed.
cards.body:
Suzan, a neighbor who lives across the street from the Fort Pierce mobile home where a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition, said she had concerns about the children's living conditions. Two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink. The kids were so hungry and starving, Suzan said. She said the children appeared unbathed and wore the same clothes every day.

Suzan said she had been inside the house and described it as unlivable. Sheets of plywood covered holes in the mobile home's floor. She said the boards visible outside the home now are the boards that were on the floor inside. Suzan said she is heartbroken thinking about the infant who lived only a few feet away and called the arrests a blessing in disguise because the children are now safe.

cards.headline: Arrests delayed nearly a year in Fort Pierce infant death as medical examiner sought outside experts
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County detectives explain why it took nearly a year to make arrests after a 3-month-old died in Fort Pierce, citing complex medical examiner work requiring outside experts.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives arrested three people Monday in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant in Fort Pierce, nearly a year after the child died in August 2025. Detective Jennifer Diaz said the case was complex and required outside expertise and months of additional testing before charges could be filed. The medical examiner sought outside experts to provide an examination for the child and those results could take several weeks or even months, Diaz said.

The infant's mother Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were charged with aggravated manslaughter and child abuse. Investigators said on Aug. 20, 2025, the 3-month-old was rushed to the hospital after the boy's grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick, but it was too late. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide. Nicole Maxwell's four other children also needed medical attention at the time and are now in foster care.

The Florida Healthcare Association said Haitian caregivers are valued members of the long term care workforce, serving as certified nursing assistants, nurses, dietary aides, housekeepers and other essential team members. According to the Lar Management Group, the Haitian community contributes an estimated $1.2 billion to Florida's economy. TPS allows people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other unsafe conditions to live and work temporarily in the United States. The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory for Haiti, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

cards.headline: Private racetrack resort community breaks ground in St. Lucie County on 650 acres
cards.teaser: P1 Motor Club is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, replacing fairways with racing circuits and preparing to welcome its first drivers this fa
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, replacing fairways with racing circuits and preparing to welcome its first drivers this fall. The private racetrack resort community features 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, compared the concept to a high-end golf resort, except with a racetrack instead of a golf course.

 The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. DuPlessis said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, with kids as young as 8 years old driving go-karts all the way up to grandparents still driving their cars on track, making it a family club.

 Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members. Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks.

 Despite the scale of the project, developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. DuPlessis said it will feel like the racetrack has been there for 100 years, comparing the scope of work to building a city. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Survey finds 64% say inflation made basics harder to afford, 42% skipped medical care
cards.teaser: A 2026 survey from eHealth found 64% of those polled say inflation has made it harder to afford basics like food, housing and clothing, with 42% saying they skipped or delayed medical care in the past year.
cards.body:
A 2026 survey from eHealth found 64% of those polled say inflation has made it harder to afford basics like food, housing and clothing, forcing many Americans to make difficult choices between necessities like rent, groceries and healthcare. The study reveals that healthcare is often losing out when people are forced to prioritize their spending.

 Medicare recipients are especially finding it challenging to afford healthcare amid rising costs. Judith Waseka, who attended a Let's Hear It community event in Vero Beach, said even with supplemental help, she and her husband are having a hard time affording their prescription drugs. "You either eat or you pay for your medication, or you sell your house or you pay for your medication," Waseka said.

 The financial pressures are leading to serious consequences for people's health. Forty-two percent of those polled say they've skipped or delayed medical care in the past year because of inflation, according to the eHealth study. This means nearly half of respondents are going without needed medical attention due to cost concerns.

 The survey highlights how inflation is forcing Americans to make impossible choices between basic necessities. When stretched budgets cannot cover housing, food and medical care simultaneously, many are choosing to forgo healthcare rather than go without shelter or meals. The findings underscore the growing financial strain facing families, particularly those on Medicare who are living on fixed incomes while trying to manage healthcare expenses that continue to rise.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks community support as husband battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound couple is asking for community support as they navigate a cancer diagnosis, holding onto faith every step of the way.
cards.body:
Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their family. Faren raised all three of their kids and home schooled. The couple started a business and had a farm where they served children.

 Years later, they moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer. As the couple searched for the right healthcare in Florida, AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource.

 Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments. The repeated visits to Orlando, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket. Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid.

 Dave, a former firefighter, had long been the family's provider. Now, Faren has stepped up to support them both, driving him back and forth from Orlando for treatment. Doctors told Dave he has an 85% chance of recovery.

 Faren works at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show their support can stop by and visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

cards.headline: Some Villa Del Sol residents return home nearly 2 years after structural damage forced evacuation
cards.teaser: Villa Del Sol residents in St. Lucie County told WPTV they are able to return home after nearly two years of being displaced from their condos following structural damage found in August 2024.
cards.body:
Residents told WPTV they were notified last month they could return to their condos, after an inspection in August 2024 found structural damage in buildings 3, 4, and 5, which were deemed unsafe. Katie Johnson was the first to share to WPTV that residents had been told they could come back. WPTV received emails sent to residents from the Board of Directors telling them they could return.

 WPTV also obtained a letter from engineers sent to St. Lucie County's Building Department requesting they lift occupancy restrictions following their special inspection. Katie Johnson described the work still underway at the property, saying they're still moving the dirt back under the buildings.

 Robert Segedin took WPTV inside his family's home, excited to return but thinking about those who cannot. Eric Johnson is among those not coming back. He was one of the first residents WPTV met at Villa Del Sol and is now living in Georgia.

 Eric Johnson said the financial toll has been severe, explaining the family had to drain out all their savings accounts and all their 401ks just trying to make ends meet while this was going on. He is filing for bankruptcy and filing his condo for foreclosure. Katie Johnson said she is thinking of neighbors like Eric Johnson who cannot return, saying she feels so bad that some were hit harder than others with the situation.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named FSL Pitcher of the Week
hero.teaser: The 22-year-old left-hander struck out 12 batters over seven scoreless innings in two appearances against Fort Myers.
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced Monday.

Ware made two appearances against the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels at Clover Park, starting Tuesday and returning for a relief outing Sunday. The left-hander combined to throw seven scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two walks while striking out 12 batters.

The Mets won both games in which Ware appeared. He earned the victory Sunday after pitching four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk and recording a career-high eight strikeouts as St. Lucie rallied for an 11-8 win.

Ware, 22, was selected by the New York Mets in the 15th round of the 2025 MLB Draft out of LSU. He made his professional debut with St. Lucie in April and has remained with the team throughout the season.

cards.headline: Mets erase 5-0 deficit to beat Mighty Mussels 11-8
cards.teaser: Jeremy Rodriguez went 4-for-4, and Conner Ware struck out a career-high eight as St. Lucie scored eight runs in the second inning.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets erased an early five-run deficit with an eight-run second inning and rallied for an 11-8 win over the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Sunday afternoon at Clover Park.

 Fort Myers won the seven-game series 4-3 and finished the season series with an 8-4 advantage.

 The Mighty Mussels scored three runs in the first inning and two more in the second to build a 5-0 lead. St. Lucie responded with eight runs in the bottom of the second and moved ahead for good.

 Randy Guzman delivered the decisive hit, lining a two-out, two-run single that turned a 5-4 deficit into a 6-5 Mets lead. Julio Zayas followed with a two-run single to extend the advantage to 8-5.

 The Mets added three runs in the third. Elian Peña hit an RBI single, Jacob Reimer drove in a run with a double and Trey Snyder added a sacrifice fly to make it 11-5.

 Conner Ware took over on the mound in the third inning and settled the game down for St. Lucie. Ware pitched four scoreless innings, allowed one hit and one walk, and struck out a career-high eight batters. He struck out the side swinging in the fourth and struck out the side looking in the sixth before earning the win.

 Fort Myers scored three runs in the seventh against Luis Sotillo, who was making his Mets debut. Sotillo recovered by retiring six of the final seven batters he faced and carried the game through the eighth inning.

 Elwis Mijares worked a perfect ninth on six pitches to record his third save.

 Jeremy Rodriguez led the Mets at the plate, going 4-for-4 with a double, an RBI and two runs scored from the No. 9 spot in the order. Zayas and Peña collected two hits apiece.

 Reimer, beginning a minor league rehabilitation assignment for a groin injury, went 1-for-3 with a double, a walk, two RBIs and two runs scored. He played all nine innings at third base.

 The Mets improved to 11-18 in the second half and 44-51 overall. They are off Monday before opening a six-game road series against the Dunedin Blue Jays on Tuesday. First pitch at TD Ballpark is scheduled for 6:30 p.m.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets Fall Short in 15-14 Loss to Fort Myers
cards.teaser: Randy Guzman hit two home runs and drove in six as the St. Lucie Mets nearly erased an eight-run deficit in a 15-14 loss to Fort Myers.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets nearly erased an eight-run first-inning deficit but fell one run short in a 15-14 loss to the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Saturday night at Clover Park.

 Fort Myers scored eight runs in the opening inning and survived several St. Lucie rallies to earn its third consecutive victory.

 Mets starter Ethan Lanthier was charged with seven runs on five hits and two walks before being removed with two outs in the first inning. Harry Genth delivered a three-run double during the Mussels' early outburst.

 Mets Answer With Five-Run First Inning

 St. Lucie immediately responded with five runs against Fort Myers starter Matt Barr in the bottom of the first. Antonio Jimenez, Branny De Oleo and Simon Juan each recorded RBI hits to cut the deficit to 8-5.

 The Mighty Mussels added three runs against Franyel Diaz in the third inning. Ramiro Dominguez drove in two with a single, and Byron Chourio hit a solo home run to extend the Fort Myers lead to 11-5.

 Trey Snyder helped St. Lucie pull closer in the fourth inning with an unconventional trip around the bases. Snyder's ground-ball single was mishandled by shortstop Quetin Young, who then committed a throwing error that allowed Snyder to score and another run to cross the plate.

 The play cut the Mussels' lead to 11-7.

 Guzman Homers Twice

 Randy Guzman hit a two-run homer against Ramiro Villanueva in the fifth inning to bring the Mets within two runs.

 Villanueva later hit consecutive batters and was ejected. St. Lucie loaded the bases with one out, but reliever Adam Falinski retired Elian Pena on a popout and Snyder on a groundout to preserve the 11-9 Fort Myers advantage.

 Young answered with a three-run home run over the batter's eye in the sixth, pushing the Mussels' lead to 14-9.

 Guzman responded again in the bottom half of the inning, launching a three-run homer to make it 14-12.

 He finished the game 3-for-4 with two home runs, a single, six RBIs and two runs scored.

 Ninth-Inning Rally Falls One Run Short

 Ricardo Paez opened the ninth inning with a solo home run that gave Fort Myers a 15-13 lead and provided what proved to be a crucial insurance run.

 Francisco Toledo scored on a wild pitch and throwing error with one out in the bottom of the ninth. Marco Vargas then homered to right field with two outs, pulling St. Lucie within one run at 15-14.

 Brent Francisco struck out Chase Meggers to end the game and record his third save.

 Michael Hilker Jr. earned the win after pitching 2 1/3 scoreless innings of relief for Fort Myers. Lanthier took the loss.

 Jimenez went 2-for-3 with two walks and three runs scored. Vargas, De Oleo and Juan added two hits apiece.

 The Mets fell to 10-18 in the second half and 43-51 overall. The Mighty Mussels improved to 14-14 in the second half and 51-42 overall.

 The teams will conclude their series Sunday at Clover Park. First pitch is scheduled for 12:10 p.m.

cards.headline: Zayas Homers Twice as St. Lucie Mets Cruise Past Mighty Mussels
cards.teaser:
Julio Zayas homered twice and Trey Snyder continued his hot stretch at the plate as the St. Lucie Mets defeated the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels 8-2 Tuesday night at Clover Park.

The
cards.body:
Julio Zayas homered twice and Trey Snyder continued his hot stretch at the plate as the St. Lucie Mets defeated the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels 8-2 Tuesday night at Clover Park.

The victory in the series opener was St. Lucie's fifth win in its last six games.

The Mets held a 1-0 lead through two innings before breaking the game open with four runs against Fort Myers starter Eric Hammond in the third.

Randy Guzman drew a bases-loaded walk to bring home the first run of the inning. Snyder followed with a two-run double before scoring on a throwing error after Antonio Jimenez singled, extending the Mets' lead to 5-0.

Jimenez added a sacrifice fly in the fifth inning to make it 6-0.

Zayas provided the rest of St. Lucie's offense with solo home runs in the sixth and eighth innings. He became the second Mets player this season to record a multi-homer game, joining Guzman.

Zayas finished 3-for-4 with his fifth and sixth home runs of the season.

Snyder also went 3-for-3 with a double, a walk, two RBIs and a run scored. He has collected seven hits over his last two games.

St. Lucie starter Conner Ware pitched three scoreless innings, allowing no runs while striking out four.

Emilio Obispo earned the win after allowing two runs on two hits over four innings. He walked three and struck out three.

Zack Mack pitched a scoreless eighth inning before Elwis Mijares worked the ninth and induced a 4-6-3 double play to end the game.

The Mets improved to 9-14 in the second half and 42-47 overall. The Mighty Mussels fell to 10-13 in the second half and 47-41 overall.

cards.headline: Messi bathed Yamal as baby in 2007 photo shoot, now they meet in World Cup final
cards.teaser: A 2007 charity calendar photo shoot paired teenage Lionel Messi with infant Lamine Yamal. Now 19 years later, they face off in Sunday's World Cup final.
cards.body:
Photographer Joan Monfort took photos in 2007 of a teenage Lionel Messi bathing infant Lamine Yamal in a plastic bathtub as part of a charity calendar produced by local newspaper Sport and UNICEF. Monfort, who works as a freelance photojournalist for The Associated Press, took the photos after Yamal's mother won a raffle of families in the city of Mataró near Barcelona who wanted to participate.

 Soccer destiny paired her baby boy with the Argentine who would become the greatest of all time. Messi left Barcelona in 2021 when the club was in financial trouble. Yamal erupted at the club two years later.

 Monfort had no recollection of the photos until Yamal's father posted one on social media during the 2024 European Championship, when a teenage Yamal led Spain to the title. The photo went viral then, but interest has skyrocketed with Sunday's World Cup final between Argentina and Spain approaching. Monfort said he has been bombarded by queries for the photos by professional media outlets while also seeing his images reproduced countless times on social media and the internet without any credit or compensation.

 The 19-year-old Yamal will face a Messi who is 20 years his senior in Sunday's final. Monfort, 58, is considering traveling to see the final in New Jersey. He said his heart is split and he does not know if he wants Messi or Yamal to win.

hero.headline: Leon County judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot
hero.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor. Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election. During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence.

Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory or more severe legal repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida. He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump.

Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent. The judge also pointed to Fishback's Florida upbringing, family relationships, driver's license, vehicle registration, voting history and work with Incubate Debate, a statewide nonprofit operating student debate programs throughout Florida. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings. Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds challenges David Jolly to three debates while Florida primary opponents remain unmet
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds issued a challenge for three general election debates with Democratic candidate David Jolly despite facing three GOP primary opponents he has not debated.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general election debates this fall, even as Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination. Jolly, a former Republican congressman now running as a Democrat, initially responded by telling Donalds to survive his own primary first. During a later CNN appearance, however, he said he would gladly meet Donalds on the debate stage a dozen times.

The exchange gave Donalds' Republican opponents Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner and businessman James Fishback another opportunity to criticize the front-runner for looking beyond them. Donalds has not debated his primary rivals while maintaining sizable advantages in polling, fundraising and endorsements. A recent Cygnal survey showed Donalds at 43 percent, compared with 12 percent for Fishback, 11 percent for Collins and 2 percent for Renner, although nearly one-third of voters remained undecided.

A separate University of North Florida poll offered an early look at the possible general election matchup. Donalds led Jolly 46 percent to 41 percent among likely midterm voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. The Aug. 18 Florida primary is less than a month away.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds pushes bill requiring AI data centers to supply their own power and water
cards.teaser: Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds introduced legislation requiring hyperscale AI data centers to provide their own power generation and water resources instead of relying on public utilities.
cards.body:
AI data centers could soon face new federal requirements under legislation backed by Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds that aims to prevent rising electricity demand from increasing utility bills for everyday customers. The proposal comes as the rapid expansion of hyperscale AI data centers raises concerns nationwide about strain on the power grid and water resources. The Electric Power Research Institute estimates data centers could consume up to 9 percent of all U.S. electricity generation by 2030, a sharp increase from current levels.

Donalds introduced H.R. 9777, known as the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require hyperscale AI data centers to provide their own power generation and water resources instead of relying on public utilities. Supporters of the proposal say it could help shield customers in Florida and across the country from future utility rate increases tied to growing energy demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure. The legislation comes as companies race to build AI infrastructure capable of supporting growing demand for generative AI systems and cloud computing.

The Trump administration recently announced the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary agreement involving major technology companies, utilities and state leaders intended to keep the cost of powering new AI facilities from being passed on to residential and commercial utility customers. The pledge has been signed by several major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI. Utilities and state leaders have also joined the initiative, according to the administration.

cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support depends on how voters are informed
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment initially, but support fell to 45 percent after voters learned of an estimated $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue.

The UNF survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment. Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years. With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal. The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot. If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. A hearing on the ballot language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County families say Florida Medicaid abruptly cut autism therapy for children
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it. Florida's health agency has not explained why.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to a critical autism therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it and Florida's health agency has not explained why. The therapy at the center of the dispute is Applied Behavioral Analysis, or ABA. The Cleveland Clinic describes it as a research-based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders, adding that many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA. Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment.

Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said her son David is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described the progress he had made through ABA, saying his vocabulary have been increasingly amazing and he can understand what is happening. Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions. Since the therapy stopped, Talia Quiroz said she has experienced dangerous regressions in her daughter's behavior. Suarez described similar physical consequences, saying she has bruised arms from one of her son's pinching.

Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country. The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Colorado. Its findings identified roughly $200 million in what it considers improper payments among the four states. A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over, across a five-year period. Questions were sent to Florida's Agency for Healthcare Administration, which runs the state's Medicaid program.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis announces Relativity Space expansion at Cape Canaveral during UK trade mission
cards.teaser: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis announced that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral during a state business development mission through England and Scotland.
cards.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis led a state business development mission through England and Scotland, opening Florida's pavilion at the Farnborough International Airshow and announcing that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral. The company plans an additional production facility for its Terran R rocket, along with expanded testing and launch infrastructure at Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. State officials say the project could create thousands of jobs by 2034. Relativity Space is also eligible for up to $134 million through Florida's Spaceport Improvement Program.

DeSantis separately oversaw a cooperation agreement between Space Florida and the U.K. Space Agency aimed at research, innovation and commercial development. In London, DeSantis and Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky met with leaders from Lloyd's of London and other insurance and reinsurance firms. The trip comes as Florida officials continue trying to attract additional private capital to the state's property insurance market. Officials said the meetings also explored a potential research partnership between Florida and the Lloyd's Lab insurance technology program.

The mission also produced new academic agreements. Florida International University and Scotland's Heriot-Watt University agreed to pursue cooperation centered on free markets, political economy and the work of Adam Smith. The University of Florida and the University of St. Andrews established a broader framework for joint research and faculty and student exchanges in fields including quantum, marine and physical sciences.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist begins 2,600-mile ride from Key West to Maine to honor friend lost to colorectal cancer
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine with a goal of raising $50,000 for young-onset colorectal cancer research.
cards.body:
A Boston cyclist is turning heartbreak into hope. After losing a close friend to young-onset colorectal cancer, Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine, with a goal of raising $50,000 for research while honoring his friend's memory. The death of his friend, who was also named Jay, inspired Weedall to honor his memory by riding his bike across the country. His goal is to raise $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center in honor of the friend he lost to the disease.

To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned for the long journey ahead. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach. Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day along the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine.

By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along those inlets. When riding hundreds of miles alone, Weedall says he has plenty of time to think. He said that even when his legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when he is a little anxious about what is going on around him, he is largely just thinking about his friend who does not get the opportunity to do this with him anymore. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

hero.headline: Indiantown Council rejects pause on data center applications despite resident pressure
hero.body:
A pair of Indiantown Village Council members failed to gain support Monday for a 90-day pause on data center applications, with village officials citing concerns about violating state law and risking millions in state funding. Councilwoman Karen Onsager proposed an administrative pause on accepting, processing and approving new applications for large-load data center development projects. The motion came after civic activist Melissa Hague renewed her request from June, telling the Council that not pausing to review land development regulations would be negligent.

Village Attorney Wade Vose said the pause would violate Senate Bills 180 and 484, repeating his legal opinion from June that such a move would put Indiantown at risk of lawsuits from property owners and developers. Vose told the Council he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney representing multiple developers within the village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit any regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed that industrially zoned lands within the village allow data centers as a permitted use.

Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer supported the concept but wanted a longer timeframe of 12 to 18 months rather than 90 days. Onsager said she chose 90 days specifically to avoid running afoul of state law and because the village is in the middle of an election cycle. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned against offending state officials who have given Indiantown over $120 million in funding. Kryzda added that when local government goes against the state or federal government, the first thing they look to do is withhold funding.

No council member seconded Onsager's motion, causing it to die. The proposal followed the withdrawal in April of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which had drawn protests from scores of local residents. Kryzda confirmed that the community meeting Onsager requested will be scheduled for Saturday, August 2, and will include technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, utility providers and relevant staff.

cards.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart in October to support youth mentoring programs
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Avia
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

 Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 According to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties, the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

 Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.
